Scope

This review is concerned with adsorbents for gas drying, that is, with the removal of water vapour from a process gas by adsorption on a solid adsorbent. In total, the review covers 145 papers published during the last 7 years. The materials involved are the three classes that are in industrial use for this duty, namely silica gel, activated alumina, and zeolite molecular sieves. The sources from which the papers are drawn are the journal and conference literature of adsorption and gas processing, and the review is confined to the subject of drying, so that studies of other separations are included only where the water behaviour of the same bed is also reported. Equilibrium studies, breakthrough studies, and studies of regeneration practice are all regarded as being in scope, since a bed has to be designed against all three of them together. The values are compared in the form in which they are published, with the method of measurement being stated wherever the method has an effect on the comparison. Capacity means the water uptake per unit mass of adsorbent at the stated partial pressure and temperature. Regeneration means the removal of the water that has been adsorbed in order to restore the capacity, whether this is brought about by means of a heated purge, by pressure reduction, or by a combination of the two.

Established results

The ordering of the isotherms of the three classes may be regarded as established. At low water partial pressures, the zeolite molecular sieves take up the greatest amount of water, and their isotherms rise steeply in this region and flatten at an early stage, so that a sieve bed is able to deliver the driest outlet. Silica gel takes up the most water in the region close to saturation, and its capacity falls steeply as the temperature rises, which makes it suited to wet feeds and to moderate specifications on the outlet. Activated alumina stands between the two in terms of affinity, is tolerant of liquid water being carried into the bed, and serves in the capacity of a guard layer ahead of sieve beds. Adsorption is an exothermic process in every class, capacity falls as the temperature rises, and the heat of adsorption warms the bed during the adsorption step, so that a bed in service is working below the capacity of its isotherm as measured at constant temperature. The practice of regeneration follows the affinity, in that temperature-swing regeneration with a heated purge is the standard approach for deep drying, pressure-swing regeneration is used for lighter duties, and the severity of regeneration that is required rises in the order from silica gel through alumina to the sieves, which is the same order as the strength with which the water is held. The working capacity in cyclic operation stands below the equilibrium capacity in all three classes, because the mass-transfer zone leaves a portion of the bed unloaded at the point of breakthrough. Beds are sized in design on the basis of the working capacity. Charges undergo ageing in service, with capacity declining over the course of cycling as a result of hydrothermal damage occurring during regeneration, contamination arising from the feed, and attrition, and this decline is at its steepest in the early part of the life of the charge.

Disagreements

The reports are in conflict on the subject of the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure. For one and the same class, and in some places for one and the same commercial grade, the uptakes that have been published at a stated low partial pressure differ from one another by more than the scatter that is claimed within each individual study. The review attributes this spread, in the main, to three features of the record. In the first place, the pretreatment differs between laboratories, since the temperature of drying, its duration, and the purge or vacuum that is applied before the measurement are not standardised, and any residual water that is left behind by a mild pretreatment will reappear in the form of a lower measured uptake. In the second place, the route of measurement differs, in that gravimetric and volumetric isotherms of a single material do not always agree with one another, and uptakes that are derived from breakthrough curves contain within them the kinetics of the particular bed and are not equilibrium values, however they may be labelled. In the third place, the basis of reporting differs, since uptake per unit mass of dry adsorbent and uptake per unit volume of bed both appear in the literature, and where the bulk density is not stated the two cannot be reconciled with one another. When attention is restricted to the values obtained from direct equilibrium measurement with the pretreatment stated, which are the values to which this review gives the greatest weight, the spread becomes narrower, although it does not disappear. The disagreement is therefore recorded as it stands: it remains unresolved, and it is at its largest precisely in the region where the drying duty is most severe and where the values are most needed.

Gaps

The measurement that nobody reports is the water uptake that is retained after extended regeneration cycling. The capacity of a fresh charge is reported fully, and capacity after a short period of cycling under mild regeneration conditions is reported on many occasions. However, the capacity after long cycling under the severity of regeneration that characterises an industrial dryer is not to be found in the record that is covered here. This gap bears on the figure against which a dryer is actually designed, namely the working capacity late in the life of the charge, from which both the size of the bed and the interval for replacement are derived. Current practice is to extrapolate the decline that is measured over short cycling, and this extrapolation remains untested against the behaviour for which it is used as a substitute. The gap also serves to conceal the balance between the severity of regeneration and the life of the charge, since more severe regeneration restores a greater amount of capacity in each cycle while consuming the structure more rapidly, and no study within the review separates these two effects from one another over an extended run. The quantity that is missing is a measurement, and one that is obtainable with standard apparatus over an extended campaign, and it is its absence that constitutes the gap recorded by this review.

Scope

This review covers adsorbents for gas drying, the removal of water vapour from a process gas by adsorption on a solid adsorbent. The review covers 145 papers from the last 7 years. The materials are the three classes in industrial use for the duty: silica gel, activated alumina, and zeolite molecular sieves. The sources are the journal and conference literature of adsorption and gas processing, and the review is confined to drying: studies of other separations are included only where the water behaviour of the same bed is reported. Equilibrium studies, breakthrough studies, and studies of regeneration practice are all in scope, since a bed is designed against the three together. Values are compared as published, with the method of measurement stated wherever the method affects the comparison. Capacity means water uptake per unit mass of adsorbent at the stated partial pressure and temperature. Regeneration means the removal of adsorbed water to restore capacity, by heated purge, by pressure reduction, or by the two combined.

The review reads each paper for the conditions as well as the values: the pretreatment before measurement, the route by which uptake was obtained, and the basis on which it is reported are recorded alongside the capacity, because the disagreements section turns on exactly those conditions and a value without them cannot be weighed.

Established results

The isotherm ordering of the three classes is established. At low water partial pressure the zeolite molecular sieves take up the most water, and their isotherms rise steeply in that region and flatten early, so a sieve bed delivers the driest outlet. Silica gel takes up the most water near saturation, and its capacity falls steeply with rising temperature, which suits it to wet feeds and moderate outlet specifications. Activated alumina stands between the two in affinity, tolerates liquid water carried into the bed, and serves as a guard layer ahead of sieve beds. Adsorption is exothermic in every class, capacity falls as temperature rises, and the heat of adsorption warms the bed during the adsorption step, so a bed in service works below the capacity of its constant-temperature isotherm. Regeneration practice follows affinity: temperature-swing regeneration with a heated purge is the standard for deep drying, pressure-swing regeneration serves lighter duties, and the severity of regeneration required rises from silica gel through alumina to the sieves, in the same order as the strength with which the water is held. Cyclic working capacity stands below equilibrium capacity in all three classes, because the mass-transfer zone leaves part of the bed unloaded at breakthrough. Design sizes beds on the working capacity. Charges age in service: capacity declines over cycling, by hydrothermal damage during regeneration, by contamination from the feed, and by attrition, most steeply early in the life of the charge.

Working capacity carries a second settled point. The mass-transfer zone lengthens as the feed grows wetter and as the cycle is shortened, so the fraction of the bed standing unused at breakthrough is a property of the duty as well as of the material. Two beds of one material, run on different duties, report different working capacities without either report being wrong, and comparisons of working capacity across duties are a recurring source of apparent contradiction in the record. Layered beds exploit the isotherm ordering directly: a guard layer of alumina or gel takes the bulk of the water where capacity near saturation governs, and a sieve layer finishes the gas where the gel isotherm has flattened, so each class works on the part of its isotherm where it is strongest.

Disagreements

Reports conflict on the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure. For the same class, and in places for the same commercial grade, the published uptakes at a stated low partial pressure differ by more than the scatter claimed within each study. The review attributes the spread, in the main, to three features of the record. Pretreatment differs between laboratories: the drying temperature, its duration, and the purge or vacuum applied before measurement are not standardised, and residual water left by a mild pretreatment returns as a lower measured uptake. The measurement route differs: gravimetric and volumetric isotherms of one material do not always agree, and uptakes derived from breakthrough curves contain the kinetics of the particular bed and are not equilibrium values, however they are labelled. The reporting basis differs: uptake per unit mass of dry adsorbent and uptake per unit volume of bed both appear, and where the bulk density is unstated the two cannot be reconciled. On the values from direct equilibrium measurement with the pretreatment stated, which this review weights highest, the spread narrows and does not vanish. The disagreement is recorded as it stands: unresolved, and largest exactly where the drying duty is most severe and the values are most needed.

Temperature control in the measurement adds a further share of the spread. Capacity falls as temperature rises, and isotherms measured without close temperature control, or reported without a temperature, enter the comparison carrying an error that belongs to the apparatus rather than to the material. The review cannot correct such values after the fact, and it weights them with the breakthrough-derived values, below the direct measurements made under stated conditions.

Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the water uptake retained after extended regeneration cycling. Fresh capacity is reported fully, and capacity after short cycling under mild regeneration is reported often. Capacity after long cycling under the regeneration severity of an industrial dryer is not in the record covered here. The gap bears on the figure a dryer is actually designed against: the working capacity late in the life of the charge, from which both the bed size and the replacement interval follow. Present practice extrapolates the decline measured over short cycling, and the extrapolation is untested against the behaviour it replaces. The gap also conceals the trade between regeneration severity and charge life, since harder regeneration restores more capacity per cycle and consumes the structure faster, and no study in the review separates the two over a long run. The missing quantity is a measurement, obtainable with standard apparatus over a long campaign, and its absence is the gap the review records.

The practical weight of the gap falls on the replacement decision. A charge is replaced when its retained capacity no longer meets the outlet specification, and the cost of the charge and of the changeover stands against the cost of the off-specification gas a spent charge passes. Both sides of that balance are estimable except the retained capacity itself, which is the quantity the literature does not supply.
